MODEL/PUBLICITY RELEASE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Taylor Morgan · photograph and name

CONSENT AND RELEASE DECLARATION
I, Taylor Morgan, consent to the use of my photograph and name by Acme Media LLC, for the following specific use(s): use in a 2026 social media advertising campaign.

Compensation for this consent: $500 flat fee

This consent covers the specific use(s) described above. It does not itself describe, and does not itself determine the effect of this consent on, any other use not described above.

THE STATUTORY CONSENT ELEMENT UNDER SECTION 3344(A) — NO WRITTEN-FORM REQUIREMENT IN THE STATUTE'S TEXT
California's living-person right-of-publicity statute makes the absence of "prior consent" part of what a plaintiff must show: liability attaches to a knowing use of another's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness "without that person's prior consent," or, for a minor, without "the prior consent of their parent or legal guardian." The statute's own text does not say that this consent must be written, signed, or take any other particular form in order to prevent liability from attaching — the operative word in the statute is "consent," unqualified by any form requirement, not "written consent." This is a fact about the statute's text as enacted; it is not a statement that an unwritten or informal consent is, as a practical or evidentiary matter, as easy to establish after the fact as a signed document, or that written consent is unnecessary or unhelpful.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "without that person’s prior consent, or, in the case of a minor, the prior consent of their parent or legal guardian"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3344(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, right of publicity — the consent element, with no written-form qualifier in the statutory text (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3344.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Civil Code section 3344, subdivision (a)(1)), used as real evidence of what that statute's own liability-creating sentence does and does not say about the form consent must take — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any particular unwritten consent did or did not occur, or would or would not be believed, in any specific dispute. This is a single statutory subdivision; no additional independent source was needed to confirm what its own text does, and does not, say. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific consent, release, or use of a name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness is valid, sufficient, or binding under Section 3344, Section 3344.1, or any other law, and completing or signing this information sheet's accompanying consent declaration does not itself resolve any of those questions or constitute legal advice about any reader's specific situation.

CONSENT HAS LIMITS: GENERAL CONTRACT-INTERPRETATION RULES, AND A CALIFORNIA SUPREME COURT CASE ILLUSTRATING A DISPUTE OVER A DIFFERENT, LATER USE
A consent or release is itself a contract, and California's general rules for interpreting contracts apply to it as they do to any other contract. Under those rules, however broad a contract's terms may be, it extends only to the things the parties actually intended to contract about, and any uncertainty left over after applying the other rules of interpretation is resolved against the party who caused that uncertainty to exist — ordinarily the party who drafted the document. Applied to a consent or release describing a specific use, these general rules mean that consent given for one described use is a factually and legally distinct question from whether consent was given for some other, different use that the document does not describe. The California Supreme Court's decision in Christoff v. Nestle USA, Inc. illustrates this distinction on real facts: a professional model was paid to pose for a photograph intended for one specific use — a label used in Canada — and the same photograph was later used, without his knowledge, in a different market and format for years afterward; the later use was treated as raising its own, separate question of consent rather than being automatically covered by whatever arrangement existed for the earlier, different use.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "However broad may be the terms of a contract, it extends only to those things concerning which it appears that the parties intended to contract."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1648 (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, a contract extends only to what the parties intended to contract about (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1648.)
  "In cases of uncertainty not removed by the preceding rules, the language of a contract should be interpreted most strongly against the party who caused the uncertainty to exist."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1654 (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, remaining uncertainty is interpreted against the party who caused it (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1654.)
  "In 1986, professional model Russell Christoff was paid $250 to pose for a photograph to be used in Canada on a label for bricks of coffee. Sixteen years later, Christoff saw his face on a jar of Taster’s Choice instant coffee in the United States and discovered that his image had been used without his consent on millions of labels sold internationally for the preceding five years."
  — Christoff v. Nestle USA, Inc., 47 Cal. 4th 468 (2009) (Cal. Sup. Ct.) — opinion's own recitation of undisputed background facts, independently fetched and verified via CourtListener's case-search index (not its full opinion text) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2597752/christoff-v-nestle-usa-inc/)

REVOCABILITY: A VALIDLY FORMED CONTRACT MAY GENERALLY BE UNDONE ONLY ON STATUTORILY SPECIFIED GROUNDS, NOT BY A LATER CHANGE OF MIND
Under California's general law of contracts, a contract requires parties capable of contracting, their consent, a lawful object, and a sufficient cause or consideration. Once a contract meeting these requirements has been validly formed, California statute lists the circumstances in which a party may rescind it: all parties can rescind by mutual agreement, or a party may rescind unilaterally where the statute allows it — for example, where that party's own consent was obtained by mistake, duress, menace, fraud, or undue influence, or where the consideration for that party's obligation fails, becomes void, or was never received. A later, unexplained change of mind by the party who gave consent is not one of the grounds this statute lists. This is a general statement about how California law treats a validly formed, consideration-supported contract; it does not itself determine whether any particular consent or release was validly formed in the first place, or whether any of the statute's listed grounds for rescission apply to any specific document or set of facts.

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1550 (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the elements essential to the existence of a contract (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1550.)

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1689(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the statutory grounds on which a contract may be rescinded (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1689.)

A MINOR'S OWN SIGNATURE: THE PUBLICITY STATUTE'S OWN PARENT-OR-GUARDIAN LANGUAGE, AND THE GENERAL RULE THAT A MINOR'S CONTRACT MAY BE DISAFFIRMED
Two separate bodies of California law bear on a minor's own capacity to consent to use of the minor's own name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness. First, Section 3344 itself does not treat a minor's own consent, standing alone, as the relevant consent for purposes of that statute: its text specifies that where the person is a minor, it is "the prior consent of their parent or legal guardian" that the statute addresses. Second, and separately, as a matter of California's general law governing minors' contracts, a contract entered into by a minor may be disaffirmed by the minor before reaching majority, or within a reasonable time afterward, or, if the minor dies within that period, by the minor's heirs or personal representative — a rule that applies to a minor's contracts generally, except where some other statute provides otherwise for a particular kind of contract. Taken together, these are two independent, factual reasons why a document recording a minor's own consent to use of the minor's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness sits differently, as a matter of California law, than the same document signed by an adult.

  "Except as otherwise provided by statute, a contract of a minor may be disaffirmed by the minor before majority or within a reasonable time afterwards or, in case of the minor’s death within that period, by the minor’s heirs or personal representative."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6710 (California Legislative Information text), California Family Code, the general rule that a minor's contract may be disaffirmed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6710.)

This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of how California's publicity statute and general minors'-contract law each separately address a minor's own consent — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific minor's consent was or was not effective, or that any specific contract was or was not disaffirmed, which depends on facts this clause does not resolve. HOW A LIFETIME CONSENT INTERACTS WITH THE SEPARATE POSTHUMOUS RIGHT UNDER SECTION 3344.1
California's posthumous right of publicity, addressed at length in this corpus's companion Right of Publicity Demand Letter document, is a legally separate statute from Section 3344, with its own rules about who may give or withhold consent after a person's death. Section 3344.1's own text specifies that the consent it requires is exercisable, after a person's death, by whoever the right of consent was transferred to under a lifetime contract, and only if no such transfer occurred does the right instead pass to the statutory successors the posthumous statute separately describes. The posthumous statute goes on to state expressly that nothing in it renders invalid or unenforceable a contract a person entered into during their own lifetime by which that person assigned, in whole or in part, the rights to use their own name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness — regardless of when that contract was signed. Read together, these provisions mean that a lifetime consent or release does not automatically bind a person's statutory successors for uses occurring after that person's death simply because the person consented to something during their lifetime; whether it does depends, under the statute's own text, on whether that lifetime document operated as an assignment of the underlying rights the posthumous statute recognizes, as opposed to a narrower permission limited to a specific use during the person's lifetime — itself a scope question of the kind addressed elsewhere in this document.

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3344.1(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, a lifetime contract assigning these rights remains valid and enforceable after death (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3344.1.)
  "The consent required by this section shall be exercisable by the person or persons to whom the right of consent, or portion thereof, has been transferred in accordance with subdivision (b), or if no transfer has occurred, then by the person or persons to whom the right of consent, or portion thereof, has passed in accordance with subdivision (d)."
  — Cal. Civ. CONSIDERATION UNDER CALIFORNIA'S GENERAL CONTRACT LAW, AND WHY THIS DOCUMENT DOES NOT RELY ON THIS CORPUS'S OTHER NO-CONSIDERATION STATUTES
California statute lists a sufficient cause or consideration among the elements essential to the existence of a contract generally, alongside capable parties, their consent, and a lawful object. The same body of law defines what counts as good consideration for a promise: a benefit conferred, or agreed to be conferred, on the promisor by someone not otherwise entitled to confer it, or a prejudice suffered, or agreed to be suffered, by that other person as an inducement to the promisor. A consent or release agreement, as an ordinary bilateral contract, is subject to this general consideration requirement unless some other, specific doctrine dispenses with it. This corpus's own trust and premarital-agreement documents separately note statutes that do dispense with the need for consideration for those particular kinds of instruments; those are express, narrow statutory exceptions to the general rule stated here, applicable to the specific instruments those statutes name, and they are not evidence that consideration is unnecessary for an ordinary consent or release agreement of the kind this document addresses.

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1605 (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the statutory definition of good consideration for a promise (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1605.)

This is one state's general contract law, used as real evidence of California's own default consideration requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific consent or release was, or was not, supported by sufficient consideration, which depends on facts this clause does not resolve. Second, and separately, as a matter of California's general law governing minors' contracts, a contract entered into by a minor may be disaffirmed by the minor before reaching majority, or within a reasonable time afterward, or, if the minor dies within that period, by the minor's heirs or personal representative — a rule that applies to a minor's contracts generally, except where some other statute provides otherwise for a particular kind of contract. Taken together, these are two independent, factual reasons why a document recording a minor's own consent to use of the minor's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness sits differently, as a matter of California law, than the same document signed by an adult.

citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided by statute, a contract of a minor may be disaffirmed by the minor before majority or within a reasonable time afterwards or, in case of the minor’s death within that period, by the minor’s heirs or personal representative.

Family Code section 6710 is itself qualified by the phrase "except as otherwise provided by statute": this document does not independently research or resolve whether some other, more specific California statute displaces the general disaffirmance rule for any particular category of contract a minor might sign, which is a real limitation on how far this clause's general statement reaches. This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of how California's publicity statute and general minors'-contract law each separately address a minor's own consent — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific minor's consent was or was not effective, or that any specific contract was or was not disaffirmed, which depends on facts this clause does not resolve. expectedJSON.body: California's posthumous right of publicity, addressed at length in this corpus's companion Right of Publicity Demand Letter document, is a legally separate statute from Section 3344, with its own rules about who may give or withhold consent after a person's death. Section 3344.1's own text specifies that the consent it requires is exercisable, after a person's death, by whoever the right of consent was transferred to under a lifetime contract, and only if no such transfer occurred does the right instead pass to the statutory successors the posthumous statute separately describes. The posthumous statute goes on to state expressly that nothing in it renders invalid or unenforceable a contract a person entered into during their own lifetime by which that person assigned, in whole or in part, the rights to use their own name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness — regardless of when that contract was signed. Read together, these provisions mean that a lifetime consent or release does not automatically bind a person's statutory successors for uses occurring after that person's death simply because the person consented to something during their lifetime; whether it does depends, under the statute's own text, on whether that lifetime document operated as an assignment of the underlying rights the posthumous statute recognizes, as opposed to a narrower permission limited to a specific use during the person's lifetime — itself a scope question of the kind addressed elsewhere in this document.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, a lifetime contract assigning these rights remains valid and enforceable after death
citations.quote: Nothing in this section shall be construed to render invalid or unenforceable any contract entered into by a deceased personality during the deceased personality’s lifetime by which the deceased personality assigned the rights, in whole or in part, to use the deceased personality’s name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness, regardless of whether the contract was entered into before or after January 1, 1985.

citations.quote: The consent required by this section shall be exercisable by the person or persons to whom the right of consent, or portion thereof, has been transferred in accordance with subdivision (b), or if no transfer has occurred, then by the person or persons to whom the right of consent, or portion thereof, has passed in accordance with subdivision (d).

expectedJSON.body: California statute lists a sufficient cause or consideration among the elements essential to the existence of a contract generally, alongside capable parties, their consent, and a lawful object. The same body of law defines what counts as good consideration for a promise: a benefit conferred, or agreed to be conferred, on the promisor by someone not otherwise entitled to confer it, or a prejudice suffered, or agreed to be suffered, by that other person as an inducement to the promisor. A consent or release agreement, as an ordinary bilateral contract, is subject to this general consideration requirement unless some other, specific doctrine dispenses with it. This corpus's own trust and premarital-agreement documents separately note statutes that do dispense with the need for consideration for those particular kinds of instruments; those are express, narrow statutory exceptions to the general rule stated here, applicable to the specific instruments those statutes name, and they are not evidence that consideration is unnecessary for an ordinary consent or release agreement of the kind this document addresses.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1550 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, sufficient cause or consideration as an element of a contract
citations.quote: It is essential to the existence of a contract that there should be: 1. Parties capable of contracting; 2. Their consent; 3. A lawful object; and, 4. A sufficient cause or consideration.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1605 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the statutory definition of good consideration for a promise
citations.quote: Any benefit conferred, or agreed to be conferred, upon the promisor, by any other person, to which the promisor is not lawfully entitled, or any prejudice suffered, or agreed to be suffered, by such person, other than such as he is at the time of consent lawfully bound to suffer, as an inducement to the promisor, is a good consideration for a promise.
